questions.q: What does the "it just needs to run once to get the number" mentality actually mean, according to this lesson?
options: The result doesn't need to be correct, just fast
The script doesn't need to be reusable, documented, or robust to other inputs — but the result it produces still has to be correct
Research code is never run more than one time in total
Only junior engineers write disposable scripts
questions.explain: A disposable script trades away reusability and robustness, not correctness. The researcher still has to trust the specific number it produces.

questions.q: Why do research codebases contain both notebooks and heavily tested shared library code?
options: It's a mistake that should be cleaned up
Exploratory code and shared infrastructure serve different purposes: fast one-off iteration versus a foundation many experiments depend on
Notebooks are banned in shared library code for licensing reasons
Shared libraries are always written in a different programming language
questions.explain: Exploratory code optimizes for iteration speed and is often thrown away; shared library code gets production-grade rigor because a bug there can invalidate many experiments at once.

questions.q: What is the one thing research teams are described as never trading away, even in the scrappiest script?
options: Code comments
Correctness of the specific result being reported
Consistent variable naming
Support for multiple operating systems
questions.explain: Robustness, reusability, and polish are negotiable. Confidence that the reported number is correct is not — a silently wrong metric creates false confidence, which is worse than no result.

questions.q: What habit does this lesson say experienced research engineers keep even in disposable scripts?
options: Writing a full test suite for every notebook cell
Sanity-checking a metric against a known baseline before trusting it
Requiring a formal code review for every plot
Never using notebooks under any circumstances
questions.explain: Sanity-checking against a baseline, printing intermediate values, and re-running surprising results are habits that persist regardless of how scrappy the rest of the script is.

questions.q: Why is scrappy, rapid experimentation kept out of shared infrastructure like the training library, according to this lesson?
options: Because shared infrastructure is owned by a different company
Because a bug introduced there can silently invalidate every experiment that depends on it that week
Because shared infrastructure is never written in Python
Because only research scientists are allowed to edit it
questions.explain: Scrappy experimentation happens in a researcher's own sandbox. Hot-patching shared infrastructure risks corrupting results for every experiment built on top of it.
